# Conformal Vacuum of dS ${}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ with Oppositely Oriented Boundaries

**Authors:** Lucas K. Kovalsky Affiliation: Quantum Algorithms and Applications Collaboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Livermore, CA, USA Shivesh Pathak Affiliation: Quantum Algorithms and Applications Collaboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Livermore, CA, USA Kyle Ritchie Affiliation: Leinweber Institute for Theoretical Physics and Department of Physics, University of California, Berkeley, California 94720, USA Affiliation: Quantum Algorithms and Applications Collaboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Livermore, CA, USA

## Abstract

We derive a dS ${}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ quotient spacetime that is asymptotically dS4, where the quotient makes its past boundary oppositely oriented relative to its future boundary. This introduces a lightlike singularity that severs the antipodes of the spacetime and simplifies its global vacuum to a trivial product on antipodal static patches. We show that this state is conformal to the vacuum of an infinite orientable cover of a non-orientable AdS3 spacetime with an S2 bundle. The vacuum’s separability extends to its holographic dual, which is a product of Cardy states. We find that this candidate dS4 vacuum state is perturbatively unstable within quantum gravity due to a vanishing Hagedorn temperature.

## I Introduction

De Sitter spacetime with $d$ -dimensions (dSd) is a maximally symmetric, time-dependent vacuum spacetime with a constant radius of curvature, $\ell$ , specified by its positive cosmological constant, $\Lambda\propto\ell^{-2}$ . The positive cosmological constant produces an accelerating universe that limits timelike observers in dSd to only have access to part of the spacetime. Antipodal observers inhabit causally independent static patches, and their future and past lightcones intersect behind cosmological horizons of area $\propto\ell$ . This causal structure produces a Euclidean vacuum that is entangled across the bifurcated horizon in a thermofield double state with temperature $\propto\ell^{-1}$ [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

This entanglement structure is difficult to describe within quantum gravity because accessing observables supported beyond cosmological horizons generally requires access to the global isometries of a spacetime [7, 8, 9]. By contrast, a string theory is more naturally restricted to the local isometries of a static patch. The holographic perspective is similarly difficult. The fact that timelike observers do not have causal influence over all of the spacetime means that de Sitter possesses spacelike boundaries, which prevent the more straightforward unitary holographic duality that timelike boundaries can offer. This means that few lessons can be applied from the AdS/CFT correspondence without significant modification [10, 11].

Compounding matters further, de Sitter spacetime exhibits exotic properties seemingly at odds with quantum gravity, including that it may support only a finite Hilbert space [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19] and its graviton propagator diverges [20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. As a result, vacuum states in de Sitter are notoriously difficult to define within quantum gravity and are frequently found to be tachyonic and unstable [25, 26, 27, 28, 29].

While the north (N) and south (S) static patches are disjoint, they share their future and past cones behind a cosmological horizon indicated by the thick diagonal crossing lines. The thin filled (dashed) lines correspond to timelike (spacelike) geodesics in the static patches.*

The more natural candidates for holographic boundaries in de Sitter are the null cosmological horizons of its static patches [4]. Exploring these has led to the so-called “monolayer” and “bilayer” proposals. [30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38]. Here we will instead flip the orientation of the past and future boundaries to disentangle antipodal static patches. This will allow restricting access of timelike observers to the local isometries of their past and future Poincaré patches. Importantly, since the boundaries of this spacetime individually remain the same as ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ , the resultant bulk geometry will be a candidate vacuum state geometry within quantum gravity.

To construct the new ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ spacetime (which we refer to as $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ with the ‘OB’ indicating “oppositely oriented boundaries”), we will use a foliation of a non-orientable $\mathbb{R}^{2,5}$ lightcone. This lightcone is useful because it can also be foliated by a non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ bundle fibered by ${\text{S}^{2}}$ in the same manner as a better-known construction for (orientable) ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ and ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times\mathbb{R}$ (with similarly oriented boundaries). Their common foliation of $\mathbb{R}^{2,5}$ establishes a conformal relationship between Rindler wedges of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ and static patches of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times\mathbb{R}$ . In its standard form, the conformal map takes the asymptotic boundary of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ to the static patch worldsheet of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times\mathbb{R}$ and is not extendable to both antipodal static patches. The holographic implications, if any, are difficult to determine [39, 40]. By instead considering the conformal map from an infinite orientable cover of non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ fibered by $\text{S}^{2}$ , we will find that we are able to leverage the new global topology to effectively extend this conformal map to both antipodal static patches of $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ with a well-defined holographic boundary.

The non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ spacetime is a recently discovered orientifold of one of its asymmetric double covers [41]. Its bulk is locally indistinguishable from ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ . Much like BTZ, it is only possible to derive it in three dimensions and is an exact solution of Einstein’s equations (i.e. it does not have singularities). Upon non-trivially fibering with ${\text{S}^{2}}$ , we will find that this space is key to determining the properties of $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ .

Finally, we will find that the separable vacuum of $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ is perturbatively unstable to excitation due to a vanishing Hagedorn temperature. It may decay to one of two degenerate ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ spacetime with similarly oriented boundaries. The latter spacetimes share the same asymptotic boundary as ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ , but with static patches that are independently conformal to Rindler wedges of orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ .

This paper is organized as follows: in Section II we review the properties of non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ and its separable Euclidean vacuum on antipodal Rindler wedges. In Section III we derive $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ and show that its Euclidean vacuum must similarly be separable on antipodal static patches. We then introduce the conformal map between one of its static patches and a Rindler wedge of non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ fibered by ${\text{S}^{2}}$ . The separability extends this conformal map piece-wise to both antipodal static patches. This allows us to develop a global holographic correspondence between bulk ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ and a conformal field theory, utilizing the AdS3/CFT2 correspondence. Finally, we discuss the implications of our derivation in Section IV.

## II ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$

In this section we review the construction of non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ ( ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ ) from a quotient of a double cover of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ . We discuss its isometry group and the structure of its asymptotic boundary. We emphasize that, when the bulk is restricted to a Rindler patch, states in the dual theory can be characterized by Cardy states associated with the two fixed-point lines on the boundary of the Rindler wedge.

### II.1 Construction

The metric for ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ in global coordinates is commonly written as

$$ {\text{d}}s^{2}=\ell^{2}(-\cosh^{2}(\rho){\text{d}}t^{2}+{\text{d}}\rho^{2}+\sinh^{2}(\rho){\text{d}}\phi^{2}), $$

where $\rho>0$ , $\phi\in[0,2\pi)$ , and $t\in\mathbb{R}$ (for its universal cover) with $\ell$ equal to ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ ’s radius of curvature.

It turns out that ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ can be rewritten in terms of global coordinates that align with the Iwasawa decomposition of ${\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}$ instead, which corresponds to the group manifold of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ :

$$ {\text{d}}s^{2}=\ell^{2}\left(-{\text{d}}\theta^{2}+{\text{d}}x{\text{d}}\theta-\frac{2x}{r}{\text{d}}\theta{\text{d}}r+\frac{{\text{d}}r^{2}}{r^{2}}\right), $$

where $r>0$ , $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ , and $x\in\mathbb{R}$ (see Appendix A for more details). $r$ is spacelike, $\theta$ is timelike, and $x$ is lightlike. Note that the (simply connected) boundary is located both at $r=0$ and $r=\infty$ , where $r=0$ is a one-dimensional patch and $r=\infty$ is a two-dimensional patch.

In this coordinate system a cylinder can be explicitly seen to be defined in $\theta$ and $x$ coordinates and it is thus straighforward to change the topology of that submanifold to a Mobius strip: $\sigma(x,\theta)=(-x,\theta+2\pi)$ . It is not possible to find such a cylinder in the usual $(\rho,r,\theta)$ coordinates because any angular coordinate will invariably be conical and introduce a conical defect after a twist. The value of the Iwasawa decomposition metric is that this twist can be performed without introducing a singularity in the bulk, since $r=0$ is also at the boundary. The lack of singularity can also be explained by the fact that there exists a (branched) double cover of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ containing this twist in the form of a $\sigma\equiv\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ subgroup [41], and ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ can also be derived by quotienting this double cover by the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ .

Yet another way to derive ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ is by using its embedding in $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ . We review this procedure as it is similar to the one we use to derive the $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ spacetime. Consider the embedding space $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ with metric $-{\text{d}}u^{2}-{\text{d}}v^{2}+{\text{d}}x^{2}+{\text{d}}y^{2}$ . In null coordinates $(u+x,v+y,v-y,x-u)\equiv(A,B,C,D)$ the metric is

$$ ds^{2}={\text{d}}A{\text{d}}D-{\text{d}}B{\text{d}}C. $$

Since the two sides of the lightcone in $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ are identical, the hyperboloid $AD-BC=\mp\epsilon$ corresponds to an ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ on either side of the $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ lightcone.

This allows for a double cover of the spacetime to be defined, whose quotient will turn out to be equivalent to a single non-orientable cover [41]. Note that the equivalence of the two sides means that Poincaré patches on one side of the lightcone can be brought to the other side isometrically (i.e. rigidly so that $(A,B,\epsilon)\rightarrow-(A,B,\epsilon)$ ). For $d\neq 2$ , this is not possible for $\text{AdS}_{d+1}$ embedded within $\mathbb{R}^{2,d}$ , since the embeddings on opposite sides of the $\mathbb{R}^{2,d}$ lightcone are not isometrically related. Moreover, it is only for $d=2$ that the isometry group factorizes into a product of two ${\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}$ s. Relatedly, working in ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ Poincaré coordinates $(\tau,x,y)$ , there are two ways of isometrically transforming Poincaré patches from one side of the lightcone to the other: 1. a simple reflection which takes ${\text{d}}s^{2}(\tau,x,y)\rightarrow-{\text{d}}s^{2}(\tau,x,y)$ , or 2. a reflection with an exchange which takes ${\text{d}}s^{2}(\tau,x,y)\rightarrow-{\text{d}}s^{2}(x,\tau,y)$ . By performing 1 and then 2, we can define a disjoint Poincaré patch on the same side of the $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ lightcone, and thereby define a new ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ , as two glued Poincaré patches related by $\tau\leftrightarrow x$ exchange. This ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ will be geometrically indistinguishable from regular ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ but will inherit a non-trivial topology.

While this looks simple enough in Poincaré coordinates, it requires a bit of extra work to relate the two Poincaré patch domains consistently to the embedding coordinates under these isometries, which is necessary to obtain the correct gluing between them.

The usual Poincaré coordinates $(\tau,x,y)$ are defined in the flat embedding coordinates $(A,B,C,D)$ as $A=1/y$ , $B=(\tau-x)/y$ , $C=(\tau+x)/y$ and $D=(-\epsilon+BC)/A=(\tau^{2}-x^{2})/y-\epsilon y$ , where $\epsilon>0$ . We begin by considering two copies of a Poincaré patch, where one is taken to the ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ hyperboloid on the other side of $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ ’s lightcone by the map $\sigma(A,B,C,D)\rightarrow(-A,-B,C,D)$ . To do this we define $\pm$ branches so that they correspond to Poincaré patches under the pre-image and image of $\sigma$ , respectively, in $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ :

$$ \displaystyle A \displaystyle=\pm 1/y,\hskip 28.45274ptB=\pm(\tau-x)/y, \displaystyle C \displaystyle=(\tau+x)/y,\hskip 28.45274ptD=(\tau^{2}-x^{2})/y-\epsilon y. $$

Note that this makes $(AD-BC)=\mp\epsilon$ , as expected from the pre-image and image of $\sigma$ , which exchanges the two sides of the $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ lightcone. Also note that $y>0$ on both branches.

As a result, the metric of the two Poincaré patches looks different compared to a pair of Poincaré patches of regular ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ :

$$ \displaystyle{\text{d}}s^{2}=\begin{cases}y^{-2}(-{\text{d}}\tau^{2}+{\text{d}}x^{2}+\epsilon{\text{d}}y^{2})&\text{for }y>0,\\
y^{-2}({\text{d}}\tau^{2}-{\text{d}}x^{2}-\epsilon{\text{d}}y^{2})&\text{for }y>0.\end{cases} $$

Specifically, these two metrics have opposite signature, which is expected, because of our earlier setup associating the two branches with opposite sides of the $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ lightcone. This also means that the domains of these two Poincaré patches do not overlap in the embedding space, despite their domains being equal in the embedded Poincaré coordinates, since each of the $\pm$ hyperboloids contain $A>0$ and $A<0)$ regions.

We proceed to isometrically transform the second (“ $-$ ” branch) Poincaré patch again so that it moves to the same side of the lightcone as the other Poincaré patch. We use the embedded coordinates to accomplish this by setting $y\rightarrow\pm y$ and $(\tau+x)\rightarrow\pm(\tau+x)$ . This sets $A=1/y$ , $B=(\tau-x)/y$ , $C=(\tau+x)/y$ and $D=(\tau^{2}-x^{2})/y\mp\epsilon y$ , where $y\gtrless 0$ . Notice that these are the same as the usual Poincaré coordinates except for the factor of $\mp\epsilon y$ in $D$ and the additional specification that $y\gtrless 0$ . Therefore, from the perspective of the embedding $(A,B,C,D)$ coordinates, this involves both a simple $(A,B,C,D)\rightarrow(-A,-B,C,D)$ reflection across its lightcone and an $\epsilon\rightarrow-\epsilon$ reflection along with $y\gtrless 0$ .

*Figure 2: ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ contains (a) a Mobius strip topology that can be seen in the two Poincaré patches. A timelike loop in its two (b) Poincaré patches returns to itself but with opposite orientation. This can be seen more clearly through its (c) orientable double cover since $\tau-x$ are exchanged after the equivalent loop.*

The effect of the $\epsilon$ changing sign on the Poincaré metric turns out to be an exchange between $\tau$ and $x$ alongside the signature flip:

$$ \displaystyle{\text{d}}s^{2}=\begin{cases}y^{-2}(-{\text{d}}\tau^{2}+{\text{d}}x^{2}+\epsilon{\text{d}}y^{2})&\text{for }y>0,\\
y^{-2}({\text{d}}\tau^{2}-{\text{d}}x^{2}+\epsilon{\text{d}}y^{2})&\text{for }y<0.\end{cases} $$

This corresponds to two Poincaré patches on the same side of $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ , which have $\tau$ and $x$ exchanged, which are now qualified to be two patches of a single ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ .

These two patches define a non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ which we refer to as ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ . Since these two patches have exchanged $\tau$ and $x$ , it can be found that a timelike observer which makes a single loop returns to themselves with opposite orientation in its tangent space; a consequence of the Mobius topology [41] (see Fig. 2a). Explicitly, for a closed cycle in the $(A,B)$ plane, e.g. $(A,B)=(R\cos\Theta,R\sin\Theta)$ , one finds that $(\partial_{A},\partial_{B})\rightarrow(-\partial_{A},-\partial_{B})\rightarrow(\partial_{A},\partial_{B})$ as $\Theta\rightarrow\Theta+2\pi\rightarrow\Theta+4\pi$ . A Penrose diagram of this spacetime with the two Poincaré patches is shown in Fig. 2b, though this is not strictly a compactification to the Einstein static universe due to the boundary topology, as we explain in the next section. Its orientable double cover can also be shown as in Fig. 2c.

In global coordinates $(\rho,t,\phi)$ , we have constructed an identification between two ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ spacetimes under $\sigma(\ell,\rho,t,\phi)=(i\ell,\rho+i\pi/2,\phi+\pi,t+\pi)$ [41]. The Wick rotation of the $\rho$ and the $\ell$ follow each other resulting in an overall minus sign, in much the same way that the opposite signature second branch Poincaré patch above was brought back to a consistent signature with the first Poincaré patch, though now oppositely oriented.

Note that it is not possible to write a global metric of a non-orientable manifold. This is because such a manifold always contains a Mobius strip topology, which requires three overlapping patches with transition functions (see the top of Fig. 2a) or two non-overlapping patches with gluing rules (see the bottom of Fig. 2a). The Poincaré patches correspond to the latter (Fig. 2b).

However, it is possible to write a global metric for the orientable double or universal cover of a non-orientable manifold. For ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ , its universal cover can be written by unrolling the $\theta$ in the compactification of the Iwasawa metric (Eq. 65):

$$ ds^{2}=\frac{dr^{2}}{r^{2}}-d\theta^{2}-\chi d\theta dr+rd\chi d\theta $$

where $\theta\in{\mathbb{R}}$ is spacelike and $\ (r,\chi)\in(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{R})\cup(\{\infty\}\times\mathbb{R})\cup\{(0,0)\}$ with $r$ timelike and $\chi$ lightlike. As before, the boundaries are at $r=0$ and $r=\infty$ . This implies that the remaining compact direction on the boundary after unrolling $\theta$ is coordinatized by $\chi$ , which is lightlike. For future reference, note that this differs from the cover obtained by unwrapping the bulk with respect to the global $t$ timelike direction instead of $\theta$ . The universal cover given by Eq. 8 is aligned with the $\sigma$ Mobius twist along the $\theta$ direction and therefore undoes it. On the other hand, the cover that unwraps $t$ does not contain the Mobius $\sigma$ twist identification as a subgroup (i.e. $t$ does not only wrap around the $r=0$ part of the boundary like $\theta$ ). While it still produces an orientable cover, we shall find that it differs on its boundary and will contain fixed points there.

Finally, for completeness we mention that the isometries of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ form the quotient group $\frac{{\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}\times{\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}}{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}$ . As discussed in the previous section, as a group manifold, ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ is ${\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}$ . There are three (orientable) double covers possible for ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ (and ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ ): the diagonal ${\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}\times{\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}$ , and the two off-diagonal $\frac{\textrm{Mp}(2,\mathbb{R})\times{\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}}{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}$ and $\frac{{\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}\times\textrm{Mp}(2,\mathbb{R})}{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}$ covers [41]. These last two differ by their chirality only. ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ ’s quotient isometry group corresponds to their quotient by $\sigma\equiv\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ .

### II.2 The Boundary of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$

The boundary of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ is orientable despite the non-orientability of its bulk [41]. Non-orientability is a global topological property, and so is not locally identifiable. As a result, the isometries of the bulk of non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ are the same as for the orientable case: $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})\oplus\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$ .

On the other hand, the $\sigma$ identification reduces the number of Killing vectors down to four at the boundary $\rho\rightarrow\infty$ :

$$ \displaystyle\chi_{0} \displaystyle=\partial_{\omega_{+}}, \displaystyle\chi_{1}^{+} \displaystyle=\exp(i\omega_{+})\partial_{\omega_{+}}, \displaystyle\chi_{-1}^{+} \displaystyle=\exp(-i\omega_{+})\partial_{\omega_{+}}, \displaystyle\chi^{-}_{1}-\chi_{-1}^{-} \displaystyle=\sin(\omega_{-})\partial_{\omega_{-}}, $$

where $\omega_{\pm}\equiv\phi\pm t$ in terms of global coordinates. These are further reduced to just three at $\omega_{-}=0,\,\pm\pi$ , generating $\mathfrak{sl}(2,{\mathbb{R}})$ .

In global ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ coordinates, we showed how the $\sigma$ identifies one ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ with another with $(\ell,\rho,t,\phi)\rightarrow(i\ell,\rho+i\pi/2,\phi+\pi,t+\pi)$ , where the transformation in $t$ and $\phi$ can be equivalently expressed as $\sigma(\omega_{+},\omega_{-})=(\omega_{+},-\omega_{-})$ .

The Wick rotation $\ell\rightarrow i\ell$ and transformation $\rho\rightarrow\rho+i\pi/2$ can be equivalently represented as $\rho\rightarrow\text{arcsinh}(\cosh(\rho))$ with $\ell$ fixed in the embedded coordinates, if their relationship to embedding coordinates is dropped. Either way, it follows that $\sigma$ exhibits “fixed points” on the $\rho\rightarrow\infty$ boundary at the lines $\omega_{-}=0$ and $\omega_{-}=\pm\pi$ , precisely where the isometries reduce to $\mathfrak{sl}(2,{\mathbb{R}})$ . The manifold is smooth at these fixed points and the Ricci scalar remains constant. However, as we shall see later, they must be excised in order to support a CFT2 [42].

The two fixed lines divide the boundary into two sections, $-\pi<\omega_{-}<0$ and $0<\omega_{-}<\pi$ , which are the same except for being oppositely oriented with respect to each other. Specifically, the $\partial_{\omega_{+}}$ null basis vector is the same in both boundary sections while the other, $\sin(\omega_{-})\partial_{\omega_{-}}$ , flips: $\partial_{\omega_{-}}\leftrightarrow-\partial_{\omega_{-}}\Leftrightarrow t\leftrightarrow\phi$ (see Figure 3).

From this perspective, due to the flip in the Killing vector between these two strips, this boundary can be equivalently described as two orientations of the same strip. Heuristically, this implies that the two strips can be thought of as the “two sides” of a two-sided (i.e. orientable) strip; the coordinates on one strip are repeated in the second strip, but with opposite relative orientation. As a result, from this perspective, the boundary is neither exterior nor interior to the bulk. This can actually be seen as the consequence of the boundary of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ ’s torus topology, which is geometrically equivalent to an orientable double cover of a Klein bottle; the cylindrical direction lies along the strips and the double cover of the Mobius strip is the perpendicular direction that cuts through both strips before coming back to itself; the fixed lines correspond to a twist and untwist (see Appendix A for more details).

*Figure 3: The two-dimensional boundary of the orientable double cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ consists of two sections separated by fixed points along $t-\phi=\omega_{-}=0,\pm\pi$ with $\partial_{\omega_{-}}$ flipped on the two sides. This can be described as two boundaries with opposite spacetime orientation, which are not causally connected because the timelike Killing vector vanishes on the fixed lines that separate them. Note that the situation is the same for its (non-orientable) single cover because the boundary is actually still orientable.*

A similar boundary can be found in self-dual ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ [43, 42], which is a $\mathbb{Z}$ quotient of one ${\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}$ chiral side of the ${\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}\times{\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}$ isometries of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ . Two lines on the boundary can be similarly found to consist of fixed points of the $\mathbb{Z}$ quotient. In both cases, this means that if the appropriate timelike coordinate is unrolled, then the remaining compact cylindrical direction on the boundary is lightlike, unlike for ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ where it is spacelike.

There is an important difference between non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ and the self-dual ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ . In both cases, $t$ and $\phi$ are bulk timelike and spacelike coordinates, and become lightlike on the boundary. However, for the self-dual ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ the fixed lines on the boundary lie on null lines on the conformal boundary [42], while for non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ , $\omega_{-}=0,\,\pi$ lie along timelike lines corresponding to $r=0$ in the Iwasawa metric (the remaining term when $r\rightarrow 0$ is timelike $\theta$ in Eq. 69-70 in Appendix A). As a result, in self-dual ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ a null coordinate lies along the strips and across the strips [42], while in ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ a timelike coordinate lies along the strips and a spacelike coordinate lies across the strips.

We will shortly be interested in an (orientable) infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ obtained by unwinding its bulk timelike dimension (specifically $t$ in the usual global coordinates) so as to compare to the universal cover of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ . This infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ is orientable and removes closed timelike curves. However, the Mobius “twist” in ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ is along its null $\theta$ direction. This means that this infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ continues to differ on its boundary from ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ .

Notably, as mentioned at the end of Section II.1, the fixed lines remain present on the boundary of the orientable infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ , since the cover does not contain the $\sigma\equiv\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ as a subgroup. Specifically, since $\omega_{-}=0,\pm\pi$ is timelike on the boundary of the single cover, the boundary of this infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ contains fixed points along its boundary spacelike dimension, $\phi=0,\pm\pi$ , too (see Fig. 4).

As a result, the bulk metric of this orientable infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ asymptotes to two boundary strips that are oppositely oriented and run up and down in the bulk timelike direction. This allows for the possibility of defining a pair of antipodal Rindler wedges so that their boundaries overlap with distinct boundary strips. As we shall see in the next section, this set-up simplifies the analysis of the relationship between the bulk and boundary in ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ .

### II.3 Holography of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$

Non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ ’s bulk classical theory can be captured by the purely topological three-dimensional Chern-Simons gauge theory with ${\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}\times{\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}$ gauge, where the action of each chiral ${\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}$ is equal to the other (multiplied by $-1$ ), unlike for orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ [44, 41]. As a result, the theory becomes a two-dimensional WZW model on its boundary defined by chiral ${\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}$ factors that have opposite signs. Here we will first show that its ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ /CFT2 correspondence implies a similar dual boundary theory based on two oppositely oriented boundary conformal field theories (BCFTs). We will then show that the ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ /BCFT2 correspondence implies a similar bulk theory to the Chern-Simons gauge theory in terms of a pair of end-of-the-world Dirichlet-branes.

As noted in the prior section, the boundary of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ is actually orientable, where each strip is oppositely oriented to the other delineated by a shared pair of lines consisting of fixed points. Despite the smoothness of the manifold, fixed points must be excised in order for a manifold to support a CFT2 [42], at which point they define a co-dimension one boundary on the boundary itself. Following Cardy [45], after excising the fixed lines, the algebra of the conformal two-dimensional manifold corresponding to each strip is reduced to a single chiral copy because the holomorphic or antiholomorphic fields that generate the pair of chiral algebras are not independent of each other at the boundary lines (i.e. they have shared boundary conditions).

In particular, for a free boson $X(\sigma,\tau)$ with spacelike $\sigma$ and timelike $\tau$ and action

$$ S=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int{\text{d}}\sigma{\text{d}}\tau\left((\partial_{\sigma}X)^{2}+(\partial_{\tau}X)^{2}\right), $$

variation of the action $\delta S$ produces the boundary term

$$ \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{B}{\text{d}}l_{B}\left(\vec{\nabla}X\cdot\vec{n}\right)\delta X. $$

Specific boundary conditions determine how each copy depends on the other. Imposing Dirichlet boundary conditions along the timelike boundary at $\sigma=0$ by setting $\delta X|_{\sigma=0}=0\Leftrightarrow\partial_{\tau}X|_{\sigma=0}=0$ , results in $j_{n}=-\bar{j}_{n}$ , where the $j_{n}$ are the $n$ th Laurent modes of $j(z)=i\partial X(z,\bar{z})$ . This aligns with the boundary WZW model where each chiral ${\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})}$ has the opposite sign compared to the other.

This contrasts with the boundary theory of self-dual ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ whose fixed points lie along a null manifold $\sigma-\tau=0,\,\pi$ (i.e. the boundary is rotated by $\pi/4$ ) [46, 42]. With such a boundary, Neumann or Dirichlet boundary conditions correspond to $\partial_{\sigma\pm\tau}X|_{\sigma-\tau=0}=0$ , which set either $j_{n}=0$ or $\bar{j}_{n}=0$ . As a result, chiral ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ ’s boundary theory consists of two chiral CFT2s with one having zero central charge [47, 48].

In ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ the two strips on the boundary corresponding to $0<\omega_{-}<\pi$ and $\pi<\omega_{-}<2\pi$ , share the same boundary conditions, albeit with flipped orientations. This means each strip can support a BCFT2, which produces a direct sum of two Hilbert spaces corresponding to opposite orientations of the same space, where each supports a state $\left|\Omega\right\rangle$ and $\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ , respectively, corresponding to a Cardy boundary (ground) states,

$$ \left|\Omega\right\rangle=\sum_{h}\sum_{N}^{\infty}\sum_{j}^{d_{h}(N)}B_{h}\left|h,N;j\right\rangle\otimes U\left|\bar{h},\bar{N};\bar{j}\right\rangle, $$

and

$$ \left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle=\sum_{h}\sum_{N}^{\infty}\sum_{j}^{d_{h}(N)}(B_{h})^{*}\left|\bar{h},\bar{N};\bar{j}\right\rangle\otimes U\left|h,N;j\right\rangle. $$

$\sum_{j}\left|h,N;j\right\rangle\otimes U\left|\bar{h},\bar{N};\bar{j}\right\rangle$ is an Ishibashi basis state with weight $h$ and level $N$ , $B_{j}$ is determined by the boundary conditions [49], and the unitary $U=I$ for diagonal CFTs.

Since the excised fixed lines at their boundaries prevent trajectories on one side from getting to the other and becoming causally dependent, the full two-dimensional boundary space supports $\left|\Omega\right\rangle\otimes\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle\equiv\left|\Omega\right\rangle\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ . As we shall find in Section II.4, taking the orientable infinite cover of this space (along the bulk $t$ timelike direction) changes the identification of $\left|\Omega\right\rangle$ and $\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ to correspond to boundary conditions that are infinitely separated, but does not change the trivial product decomposition of $\left|\Omega\right\rangle\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ .

As first noted in the previous section, a bulk Rindler wedge (and its antipode) can be defined such that its boundary overlaps with only one strip (and the opposite strip; see Fig. 4). It is well-known that a Rindler wedge corresponds to the bulk region that is causally connected to its boundary causal diamond. Redefining the state $\left|\Omega\right\rangle$ to be restricted only on the boundary of a Rindler wedge, and $\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ to be restricted on the boundary of its opposite orientation, each $\left|\Omega\right\rangle$ and $\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ state can be considered to correspond to an open string restricted to the Rindler wedge’s boundary.

A Rindler wedge (red in Fig. 4) and its antipodal counterpart (blue in Fig. 4) are connected in ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ by closed timelike curves. Taking the orientable infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ by unwinding the $t$ dimension removes these closed curves so that antipodal Rindler wedges (e.g. red and blue) are no longer timelike separated. Importantly, the boundary fixed lines remain present.

*Figure 5: (a) The orientable infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ with unwrapped $t$ with annotated boundary $\left|\omega\right\rangle$ , $\left|\bar{\omega}\right\rangle$ and corresponding bulk $\left|\Omega\right\rangle$ , $\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ states, respectively. (b) The Penrose diagram of the orientable double cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ . The blue and red diamonds show the conformal projection of the two antipodal Rindler patches in Poincaré patch $P_{1}$ shown in Fig. 4 (note that these Rindler patches do not “fill out” the dropped dimensions at most points; one Rindler patch is “in front” of the other). $\left|\omega\right\rangle$ and $\left|\bar{\omega}\right\rangle$ are bulk states defined on antipodal Rindler patchs with boundary dual states $\left|\Omega\right\rangle$ and $\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ , respectively.*

As a result, in this infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ , a Rindler wedge and its antipode’s boundaries continue to overlap with different strips after they are no longer connected by closed timelike loops. This means that they are now purely spacelike separated, but also that their bulks asymptote to oppositely oriented boundaries, which support unentangled Hilbert spaces. We proceed to study the effect of these distinct asymptotic regions in the bulk Rindler states using the framework of the AdS/BCFT duality, where the bulk dual of a single strip of the boundary CFT, say between $\omega_{-}\in(0,\pi)$ , can be found by evaluating the gravitational path integral with an end-of-the-world (EOW) brane through the bulk [50]. We will find that the symmetry of the CFT boundary conditions results in a tensionless geodesic brane through the diameter of AdS.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ denote the bulk dual manifold whose boundary consists of an asymptotic component, denoted $\mathcal{B}$ , and a brane component, denoted $Q$ , so that $\partial\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{B}\cup Q$ . The brane obeys a homology constraint, such that its boundary coincides with the boundary of $\mathcal{B}$ , i.e. with the fixed lines on $\partial\mathcal{M}$ . Denoting the lines (upon which Dirichlet conditions are imposed) by $D_{0}$ and $D_{\pi}$ , this means that $\partial Q=\partial\mathcal{B}=D_{0}\cup D_{\pi}$ . The EOW brane is found via the saddle-point approximation to the gravitational path integral, e.g. by extremizing the Einstein-Hilbert action

$$ S=\frac{1}{16\pi G_{N}}\int\limits_{\mathcal{M}}\sqrt{-g}(R-2\Lambda)+\frac{1}{8\pi G_{N}}\int\limits_{\partial\mathcal{B}}\sqrt{-h}K+\frac{1}{8\pi G_{N}}\int\limits_{Q}\sqrt{-h}(K-T) $$

where we have assumed that the matter contribution to the brane action is due solely to tension $T$ , i.e. $T_{ab}^{matter}=Th_{ab}$ . The brane equation of motion is well-known:

$$ K_{ab}-\frac{1}{2}Kh_{ab}=-8\pi G_{N}Th_{ab} $$

where $K_{ab}$ is the extrinsic curvature of $Q$ and $h_{ab}$ is the induced metric on $Q$ .

Taking our ansatz bulk geometry to be that of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ , or equivalently ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ (these geometries can be locally identified within a single Poincare patch), it can be straightforwardly verified that, in global coordinates, the brane is parameterized by

$$ \sinh\rho\sin\phi=\sinh\rho_{*} $$

where the $\rho_{*}$ is related to the brane tension via

$$ T=\frac{1}{L}\tanh\rho_{*} $$

specifically, the range of $\phi$ is covered by two branches:

$$ \phi(\rho)=\left\{\begin{matrix}\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sinh\rho_{*}}{\sinh\rho}\right),&\rho\in(\rho_{*},\infty)\\
\pi-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sinh\rho_{*}}{\sinh\rho}\right),&\rho\in(\rho_{*},\infty)\end{matrix}\right. $$

Since completely reflecting (i.e. Dirichlet) conditions on $D_{0}$ and $D_{\pi}$ are necessary to ensure the factorization of the CFT vacuum, and since $D_{0}\cup D_{\pi}=\partial Q$ , this suggests that Dirichlet conditions must be imposed on the entirety of $Q$ . This suggests that we take the tensionless limit, i.e. $\rho_{*}\rightarrow 0$ , resulting in a timelike brane that bisects ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ :

$$ \phi(\rho)=\left\{\begin{matrix}0,&\rho\in(0,\infty)\\
\pi,&\rho\in(0,\infty)\end{matrix}\right. $$

This brane intersects every constant time slice $t=t_{0}$ at precisely the edge of the bulk domain of dependence of the boundary $t=t_{0}$ slice between $D_{0}$ and $D_{\pi}$ . That is, on the $t=t_{0}$ slice, it coincides with the bifurcate Rindler horizon of the region dual to the $t_{0}$ slice of the BCFT.

Since the bulk dual to the CFT supported on the $\omega_{-}\in(0,\pi)$ terminates at the brane, this immediately implies that the bulk vaccuum is supported on Cauchy slices which terminate at the brane. Consequently, the vacuum is supported on a single Rindler wedge. In particular, if the state $\left|\Omega\right\rangle$ is supported on region $\omega_{+}=0,\omega_{-}\in(0,\pi)$ , then its bulk dual is a pure state $\left|\omega\right\rangle$ supported on corresponding Rindler wedge.

However, our BCFT does not consist solely of a single CFT in the region $\omega\in(0,\pi)$ . A second non-interacting copy lives on the $\omega\in(-\pi,0)$ region. One finds an identical set of bulk branes, and in the tensionless limit, the brane coincides with the bisecting brane discussed above. Likewise, the BCFT state $\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ supported on $\omega_{+}=0,\omega_{-}\in(-\pi,0)$ is dual to a bulk state $\left|\bar{\omega}\right\rangle$ supported on the Rindler wedge antipodal to that supporting $\left|\omega\right\rangle$ . In particular, the bulk dual to the BCFT product state $\left|\Omega\right\rangle\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ is the state $\left|\omega\right\rangle\left|\bar{\omega}\right\rangle$ supported on antipodal Rindler wedges. The lack of entanglement in the bulk vacuum is a consequence of the Dirichlet boundary conditions imposed on the bisecting brane.

Finally, note that although we have performed the brane calculation for each BCFT half separately, since the boundary conditions are symmetric, we could regard them as living on two halfs of a shared manifold, which is glued along the brane. In particular, the Dirichlet conditions on the shared BCFT boundary $D_{0}\cup D_{\pi}$ ensures that we can equivalently regard the two CFT’s as either living on two halves of a single CFT manifold with Dirichlet conditions imposed on the surface $D_{0}\cup D_{\pi}$ , or as two “disconnected" CFTs supported on half spaces $\mathcal{B}$ and $\bar{\mathcal{B}}$ each ending at $\partial\bar{\mathcal{B}}=\partial\mathcal{B}$ , with bulk duals $\mathcal{M}$ and $\bar{\mathcal{M}}$ each ending on $Q$ , and which are subsequently glued along their boundaries. This is depicted in Fig. 6

The dashed lines depict brane solutions of Eq. 18 with nonvanishing tension. The solid lines depict the tensionless branes. In the tensionless limit with Dirichlet conditions on the branes, the two bulk regions can be regarded as glued along their shared boundaries.*

To summarize, the state $\left|\omega\right\rangle$ (or $\left|\bar{\omega}\right\rangle$ ) corresponds e.g. to the red (blue) bulk Rindler wedges in (a) of the orientable infinite cover depicted in Fig. 4, and $\left|\Omega\right\rangle$ (or $\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ corresponds to state on the the red (blue) boundary diamonds depicted in (b) of the same figure. Furthermore, since a pair of Rindler patches contains a global spatial slice of the full ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ spacetime, $\left|\omega\right\rangle\left|\bar{\omega}\right\rangle$ must correspond to a bulk vacuum state of the orientable infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ , which is dual to the CFT2 ground state $\left|\Omega\right\rangle\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ .

### II.4 Instability of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ to Quantum Gravity Dynamics

The two fixed lines (i.e. boundary conditions) in ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ have a finite proper distance between them before $t$ is unwrapped. This means that in the corresponding two-dimensional conformal manifolds, where these fixed lines are excised, the length between them is finite in the ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ target space.

As previously discussed, $\omega_{-}$ becomes spacelike (and so $\omega_{+}$ becomes timelike) on the boundary of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ . As a result, when $t$ is unwrapped to produce an orientable infinite cover of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ , only $\omega_{+}$ is unwrapped on the boundary (see Fig. 7). However, since unwrapping one dimension of a CFT2 with boundary is conformally equivalent to unwrapping both dimensions (see Fig. 7d), unwrapping $\omega_{+}$ also elongates the finite proper distance in $\omega_{-}$ between the fixed lines in the ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ target space to infinity.

*Figure 7: a) The (single cover of the orientable) boundary of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ is shown with periodic spatial direction (red arrow) and finite-length timelike direction (blue arrow). These can be considered as supporting a finite-length open string (blue) and closed string (red), respectively. b) This means that each strip is equivalent to a cylinder topology with a finite width. c) The infinite cover with respect to $t$ unwraps the boundary’s periodic timelike (red) direction. The remaining compact direction is lightlike instead of spacelike, unlike in the universal cover of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ . d) Unwrapping makes each strip topologically equivalent to an infinite strip. Since this is conformally equivalent to the half-plane, it is the worldsheet of an open string (blue) or closed string (red) extending to infinite length.*

As a result, unwrapping $t$ separates the boundary conditions so that the proper distance between a fixed point line $\omega_{-}=0$ and the former $\omega_{-}=\pm\pi$ becomes infinite and the corresponding open string length $\alpha\rightarrow\infty$ . The Cardy formula,

$$ \rho(L_{0})\sim e^{2\pi\sqrt{\frac{cL_{0}}{6}}}, $$

reveals that for bosonic string excitations at level $n$ with $m^{2}\sim E\sim n/\alpha$ , we have $\rho(E)\sim\exp(\tilde{c}E\sqrt{\alpha})$ . With $T=({\frac{\partial S}{\partial E}})^{-1}$ , the Hagedorn temperature becomes $T_{H}\sim\alpha^{-1/2}\rightarrow 0$ [51]. Hence, this CFT2 has vanishing Hagedorn temperature and is unstable to all excitation above the vacuum state.

A similar instability can be found for AdS2 and self-dual AdS3 as a consequence of the null energy condition [46]. Long strings have been studied in these contexts [40].

### II.5 $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ Construction

To study the global vacuum of the ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ fiber bundle in the next section, we will use a conformal map between its static patches, and Rindler wedges of $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ . We take a brief detour to introduce this larger fibered space of non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ .

Recall that ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ can be represented as an embedded surface in $\mathbb{R}^{2,2}$ as either $-u^{2}-v^{2}+x^{2}+y^{2}=-\epsilon$ or $-u^{2}-v^{2}+x^{2}+y^{2}=\epsilon$ , with $\epsilon>0$ , and these two constraint equations are related to one-another by the map $\sigma(u,v,x,t)=-(x,y,u,v)$ . This relationship was used to construct ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ via a quotient of a double cover of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ by the map $\sigma$ . To construct a non-orientable $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ , we similarly observe that ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ may be embedded into an $\mathbb{R}^{2,5}$ lightcone via the following constraint equations:

$$ \displaystyle\underbrace{-u^{2}-v^{2}+x^{2}+y^{2}}_{=-\epsilon}+\underbrace{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}_{=+\epsilon} \displaystyle=0. $$

As in the three-dimensional case, an opposite signature ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ can be embedded into a partially Wick-rotated lightcone by changing the sign of $\epsilon$ in the embedding equations:

$$ \displaystyle\underbrace{-u^{2}-v^{2}+x^{2}+y^{2}}_{=+\epsilon}+\underbrace{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}_{=-\epsilon} \displaystyle=0. $$

These constraints are related to the previous ones by simultaneously performing $\sigma(u,v,x,y)=-(x,y,u,v)$ along with a Wick rotation of the $(a,b,c)$ coordinates. By constructing an appropriate double cover of the $\mathbb{R}^{2,5}$ lightcone, and quotienting by a map which simultaneously exchanges the ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ coordinates and Wick rotates the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ coordinates, we can obtain a non-orientable fiber bundle space, $(\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)},{\text{AdS}_{3}},\pi,{\text{S}^{2}})$ , such that the continuous surjective map $\pi:\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}\rightarrow{\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ behaves like a projection from the corresponding regions of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\rightarrow{\text{AdS}_{3}}$ on each Poincaré patch, which we denote by $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ . See Appendix B for more details.

Compared to ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ , the two glued Poincaré patches are augmented by ${\text{S}^{2}}$ product spaces: the $y>0$ patch is accompanied by an ${\text{S}^{2}}$ space while the $y<0$ patch (with exchanged $\tau$ and $x$ ) is accompanied by an oppositely oriented ${\text{S}^{2}}$ space. The resultant metric is

$$ {\text{d}}s^{2}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{y^{2}}\left(-{\text{d}}\tau^{2}+{\text{d}}x^{2}+\epsilon{\text{d}}y^{2}\right)+\epsilon{\text{d}}\Omega_{2}^{2},&y>0,\\
\frac{1}{y^{2}}\left(-{\text{d}}x^{2}+{\text{d}}\tau^{2}+\epsilon{\text{d}}y^{2}\right)+\epsilon{\text{d}}\bar{\Omega}_{2}^{2},&y<0,\end{cases} $$

where the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ factor with metric ${\text{d}}\bar{\Omega}_{2}$ is antipodally parameterized by $(\pi-\theta,2\pi-\phi)$ . Therefore, we see that the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ appears as a non-trivial fiber, rather than as a separate, non-orientable factor.

*Figure 8: The Penrose diagram of the orientable double cover of $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ . The blue and red diamonds show the projection of the two antipodal Rindler patches in Poincaré patch $P_{1}$ shown in Fig. 4 (note that these Rindler patches do not “fill out” the dropped dimensions at most points).*

The only new aspect of the $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ topology (compared to just non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ ) is the non-trivial fibering of the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ factor. However, this does not make the spacetime non-orientable in this factor; a path that completes a $2\pi$ loop in non-spacetime-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ necessarily finds that its dimensions in the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ factor have returned to their original orientation due to the fibering. This can be seen in the Penrose diagram of the orientable double cover of $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ (see Fig. 8) where the sign of $r$ (i.e. the orientation of the two-sphere) flips along with the sign of $y$ and not with the $\tau-x$ exchange.

As a result of the added ${\text{S}^{2}}$ fiber, the structure of $\left|\omega\right\rangle$ and $\left|\bar{\omega}\right\rangle$ may change. However, given that the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ vanishes at the ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ boundary (i.e. $y\rightarrow 0$ makes the ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ metric infinitely larger than the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ in Eq. 26), the $\left|\Omega\right\rangle$ and $\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ are expected to remain unchanged as Cardy states. Specifically, the Brown-Henneaux conditions for ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ with global metric ${\text{d}}s^{2}=-f(r){\text{d}}t^{2}+f^{-1}(r){\text{d}}r^{2}+r^{2}{\text{d}}\theta^{2}$ [52] are:

$$ \displaystyle g_{AB} \displaystyle=r^{2}\gamma_{AB}+\mathcal{O}(1), \displaystyle g_{rA} \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(r^{-3}), \displaystyle g_{rr} \displaystyle=\frac{\ell^{2}}{r^{2}}+\mathcal{O}(r^{-4}), $$

where $\gamma_{AB}$ is a fixed metric on the cylinder at spatial infinity $r\rightarrow\infty$ and $x^{A}=(t,\theta)$ . $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ satisfies these conditions since the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ bundle can be considered to add as a $\mathcal{O}(r^{-2})$ factor in $g_{AB}$ , which is contained in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ .

Regardless, the holographic correspondence between bulk $\left|\omega\right\rangle$ and $\left|\bar{\omega}\right\rangle$ states and boundary $\left|\Omega\right\rangle$ and $\left|\bar{\Omega}\right\rangle$ states, respectively, remains the same (see Fig. 8).

## III $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$

In this section we will derive a de Sitter spacetime, with product space $\mathbb{R}$ , and examine its properties within quantum gravity. We proceed with a derivation in Section III.1. We will examine the oppositely oriented boundaries of this spacetime and show their consequences on the static patches. Otherwise, we show that the de Sitter spacetime shares the same boundary as regular ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ . Finally, in Section III.2 we discuss its bulk/boundary correspondence by utilizing a generalization of the conformal map between static patches of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ and Rindler wedges of the universal cover of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ .

### III.1 $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ Construction

Consider the $\mathbb{R}^{2,5}$ lightcone used in the construction of $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ . Rather than embedding ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ via the restrictions given by Eqs. 24-25, we instead impose ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times\mathbb{R}$ restrictions via the following constraint equation:

$$ \displaystyle\underbrace{-u^{2}+x^{2}+a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}_{=+\epsilon}\underbrace{-v^{2}+y^{2}}_{=-\epsilon} \displaystyle=0. $$

We do not expect $\sigma$ to be a subgroup of the bulk isometries of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ or its higher covers. This is easy to verify by noting that it cannot be expressed in global coordinates of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ (see Appendix C).

However, it can be found to be expressible in terms of Poincaré coordinates of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ . In fact, we shall find that $\sigma$ should only be considered as producing orbifold spacetimes when considered over Poincaré patches (or subpatches thereof) of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ . In other words, $\sigma$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ subgroup of a double cover (of a subgroup) of the bulk isometry group $\text{SO}^{+}(1,3)\times{\mathbb{R}}$ of either pair of Poincaré patches of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ but not of the bulk isometry group $\text{SO}^{+}(1,4)\times{\mathbb{R}}$ of global ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ (or any higher covers). Specifically, we shall find that $\sigma$ does not preserve the $\text{SO}(4)$ isometry of the ${\text{S}^{3}}$ of ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ ’s global topology, but does preserve the local $\text{SO}(3)$ isometries of the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ s fiber bundle over ${\text{S}^{1}}$ that makes up ${\text{S}^{3}}$ . Poincaré patches only contain the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ ’s on half of the ${\text{S}^{1}}$ , and so contain the $\sigma$ as a subgroup of a double cover of their bulk isometries. Therefore, there is only a meaningful orbifold formed when taking a quotient of Poincaré patches of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ (or subpatches thereof).

Let us specifically consider flat slicing coordinates on $u+x>0$ where the $u=\ell\sinh(t/\ell)+\frac{r^{2}e^{t/\ell}}{2\ell}$ , $x=\ell\cosh(t/\ell)-\frac{r^{2}e^{t/\ell}}{2\ell}$ , and $a=e^{t/\ell}y_{i}$ etc., for $r^{2}=\sum_{i}y_{i}^{2}$ , and hyperbolic coordinates for ${\mathbb{R}}$ : $v=\ell\cosh(\phi)$ and $y=\ell\sinh(\phi)$ . The time coordinate in Poincaré coordinates corresponds to $\eta=\eta_{t=\infty}-\ell e^{t/\ell}$ . Projected onto the embedded manifold’s coordinates, $\sigma$ can be expressed by

$$ \ell\rightarrow i\ell,\,t\rightarrow it-\frac{\pi}{2}\ell,\,\phi\rightarrow\phi+i\frac{\pi}{2},\,y_{i}\rightarrow y_{i}. $$

Choosing instead the other Poincaré patch with the same spacelike boundary involves taking $x\rightarrow-x$ and so requires changing $\sigma$ ’s definition to

$$ \ell\rightarrow-i\ell,\,t\rightarrow-it+\frac{\pi}{2}\ell,\,\phi\rightarrow\phi-i\frac{\pi}{2},\,y_{i}\rightarrow y_{i}. $$

The expanding Poincaré patch with $u+x>0$ and the other expanding Poincaré patch with $u-x>0$ are partially overlapping. Quotienting by $\sigma$ independently preserves a subgroup of each patch’s isometry group. However, the resultant two spaces are no longer covers of the same global space and should be considered to be two different quotients of the same ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ spacetime that splits it up into two different pairs of spaces.

Another way to see this is by noting that when $\sigma$ is projected onto embedded Poincaré coordinates it introduces fixed points along their Poincaré horizons. Since $\sigma$ is not a subgroup of the global isometry group of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ , these fixed points actually correspond to points of geodesic incompleteness, i.e. singularities. Singularities cannot be observer-dependent. Specifically, we can find from Eqs. 31-32 that $\sigma$ introduces fixed points at $t/\ell\rightarrow\pm\infty$ , $\phi\rightarrow\pm\infty$ . Since the “extra” fifth dimension coordinatized by $\phi$ is conformally suppressed by $\eta$ at the Poincaré spacetime boundaries, only the $t/\ell\rightarrow-\infty$ , $\phi\rightarrow\pm\infty$ fixed points are reachable. This corresponds to a lightlike singularity on the Poincaré horizon at $\phi=\pm\infty$ . This is true of either pair of contracting and expanding Poincaré patches of the spacetime (see Fig. 9). Since the Poincaré horizon contains “naked” singular points, in order to have well-defined Hamiltonian evolution from past Cauchy slices, we place Dirichlet conditions along the entire Poincaré horizon. This is also compatible with the change in the orientation of the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ at the Poincaré horizon.

As a result, it is not possible to express Eq. 31 in terms of the $u-x\lessgtr 0$ Poincaré patches directly (i.e. without going through the embedding space) because it breaks up the $u-x\lessgtr 0$ Poincaré patches along the former’s singular Poincaré horizon. Similarly, Eq. 32 can be found to break up the $u+x\lessgtr 0$ Poincaré patches. Therefore, though Eq. 31 and Eq. 32 can both be inferred from $\sigma$ when it is expressed in embedding coordinates, it corresponds to multiple distinct operations in embedded coordinates, and produce different quotient spacetimes depending on which covering space of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ is initially considered.

Considering Eq. 30 along with its opposite constraint,

$$ \displaystyle\underbrace{-u^{2}+x^{2}+a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}_{=-\epsilon}\underbrace{-v^{2}+y^{2}}_{=+\epsilon} \displaystyle=0. $$

allows us to proceed in a similar manner to before to define this new spacetime (see Appendix D). The result is

$$ {\text{d}}s^{2}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}\left(-{\text{d}}\eta^{2}+{\text{d}}X^{2}+X^{2}{\text{d}}\Omega_{2}^{2}+\eta^{2}L^{2}{\text{d}}\phi^{2}\right),&\eta>0,X>0,\phi\in{\mathbb{R}},\\
\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}\left(-{\text{d}}\eta^{2}+{\text{d}}X^{2}+X^{2}{\text{d}}\Omega_{2}^{2}+\eta^{2}L^{2}{\text{d}}\phi^{2}\right),&\eta<0,X<0,\phi\in{\mathbb{R}}.\end{cases} $$

This metric describes two opposite Poincare patches, i.e. the expanding region for $\eta>0$ and the contracting region for $\eta<0$ , with oppositely oriented bulk ${\text{S}^{2}}$ s and parity-flipped fifth spatial dimensions, respectively. The opposite orientation of the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ factors is revealed by the fact that $X<0$ in the second branch, although now this flips the orientation of the spatial ${\text{S}^{3}}$ , since $X\in\mathbb{R}$ and is not fixed. By this we mean that, in spherical coordinates, if the $X>0$ portion of the ${\text{S}^{3}}$ is coordinatized by $(X,\theta,\phi)$ for $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ , $\phi\in(0,2\pi)$ , then the $X<0$ portion of the ${\text{S}^{3}}$ coordinatized by $(X,\theta,\phi)$ is equivalently described by $(X,\pi-\theta,2\pi-\phi)$ with $X>0$ , and therefore has opposite orientation.

It is important to note that, unlike $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ , the oppositely oriented ${\text{S}^{2}}$ s appear within the ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ geometry, rather than as a non-trivial fiber attached to ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ . Rather, it is the ${\mathbb{R}}$ factor which is fibered with the ${\text{OB-dS}_{4}}$ , but unlike the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ , it appears as a trivial factor.

*Figure 9: Penrose diagram of two $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ quotient spacetimes, corresponding to Eq. 31 and Eq. 32, composed of expanding and contracting Poincaré patches. Regardless of which quotient spacetime is considered, antipodal static patches only experience one orientation of ${\text{S}^{3}}$ , e.g. the blue patch only sees $X<0$ while the red patch only sees $X>0$ . A lightlike singularity exists at the horizons of the Poincaré patch.*

Finally, let us determine the bulk isometries of $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ . We can start with the bulk isometries of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ and find that there are only four isometries that survive the quotient with $\sigma$ :

$$ \displaystyle\chi_{1} \displaystyle=u\partial_{x}+x\partial_{u} \displaystyle=\ell\cos\theta\cosh\frac{2t}{\ell}\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\ell^{2}\sin\theta\sinh\frac{2t}{\ell}\partial_{\theta} \displaystyle\chi_{2} \displaystyle=v\partial_{y}+y\partial_{v} \displaystyle=\ell\cosh\frac{2\phi}{\ell}\partial_{\phi}, \displaystyle\chi_{3} \displaystyle=u\partial_{v}-v\partial_{u}+x\partial_{y}-y\partial_{x} \displaystyle=\ell\left(\sinh\frac{t}{\ell}\sinh\frac{\phi}{\ell}(\partial_{\phi}-\cosh\theta\partial_{t})\right. \displaystyle\qquad\left.+\cosh\frac{t}{\ell}\left(\cosh\frac{\phi}{\ell}(-\partial_{t}+\cos\theta\partial_{\phi})+\ell\sin\theta\sinh\frac{\phi}{\ell}\partial_{\theta}\right)\right), \displaystyle\chi_{4} \displaystyle=u\partial_{y}+y\partial_{u}+x\partial_{v}+v\partial_{x} \displaystyle=\ell\left(\sinh\frac{t}{\ell}\cosh\frac{\phi}{\ell}(\partial_{\phi}+\cosh\theta\partial_{t})\right. \displaystyle\qquad\left.+\cosh\frac{t}{\ell}\left(\sinh\frac{\phi}{\ell}(\partial_{t}+\cos\theta\partial_{\phi})-\ell\sin\theta\cosh\frac{\phi}{\ell}\partial_{\theta}\right)\right). $$

Like in the case of $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ on the boundary, these form $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})\oplus\mathbb{R}$ (though in the bulk). $\chi_{4}$ vanishes at $\theta=0$ and $t=-\phi$ or $\theta=\pi$ and $t=\phi$ , reducing the isometries to just $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$ .

It remains to verify that the boundaries of $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ qualify as asymptotically ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ despite the extra fifth dimension and its separation into two oppositely oriented Poincare patches. As already pointed out, it turns out that the fifth dimension coordinatized by $\phi$ is not supported on these boundaries because it is conformally suppressed. To see whether the conformal suppression is rapid enough not to affect the asymptotic symmetries, we can analytically continue the Brown-Henneaux boundary conditions from AdS4 to de Sitter with global metric ${\text{d}}s^{2}=\frac{\ell^{2}}{\cos^{2}t}(-{\text{d}}t^{2}+{\text{d}}\Omega_{3}^{2})$ . This reveals that since $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ ’s ${\mathbb{R}}$ factor is independent of $t$ , the only Brown-Henneaux condition that needs to be verified is $g_{AB}=(t\mp\pi/2)^{-2}\gamma_{AB}+\mathcal{O}(1)$ , where $\gamma_{AB}$ is the fixed metric on the spatial sphere at timelike infinity ( $t\rightarrow\pm\pi/2$ ) and $x^{A}=(r,\Omega_{2})$ [10]. This condition is clearly met by both $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ and regular ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ . The same is true of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\text{S}^{1}}$ , which we will discuss later.

As for the effect of the opposite orientations caused by the $\sigma$ quotient, since we know this the quotient with $\sigma$ reduces the bulk isometries to minimally $\mathfrak{sl}(2,{\mathbb{R}})$ , it qualifies only as an asymptotically ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ with similarly reduced asymptotic symmetries. This is similar to the way that ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ is asymptotically ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ despite only containing minimally an $\mathfrak{sl}(2,{\mathbb{R}})$ and its associated chiral Virasoro algebra.

In general, asymptotic symmetry spaces with reduced symmetries contain singularities that can be associated with the insertion of point particles with mass that have broken the removed isometries. As a result, these are usually excited states (e.g. BTZ compared to ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ ). We shall soon see that perhaps a similar situation holds for $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ , when it is identified as a false vacuum state at higher energy than the true vacuum state, where the singularities act as point particles.

### III.2 The Bulk/Boundary Correspondence

Since $\sigma$ is a subgroup of a double cover of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ ’s bulk isometry group, it can only produce fixed points on the boundary of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ . This is similar to the case for self-dual ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ , and as we found, both spaces have fixed points along two co-dimension one manifolds on their boundaries. Since we do not expect $\sigma$ to also be a subroup of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ or any of its covers, it should break the bulk spacetime into at least two manifolds.

We found in the previous section that the spacetime consists of two oppositely ${\text{S}^{2}}$ -oriented Poincaré patches with singularities at their horizons. The original original ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ spacetime is severed along its Poincaré horizons (see Fig. 9) precisely because the $\sigma$ is not a subgroup of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ , and its quotient flips the orientation of the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ s of the two Poincaré patches of $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ .

Note that, as shown in Fig. 9, antipodal static patches only experience one orientation of ${\text{S}^{2}}$ regardless of which pair of contracting and expanding Poincaré patches are chosen to cover $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ . Heuristically, this is because the orientation they experience is uniquely determined by the singularity they asymptote to, and this singularity is contained in their Poincaré patch regardless of whether it is contracting or expanding.

Excising the Poincaré patch horizons allows us to now describe the structure of $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ in terms of two disjoint Poincaré patches. If boundary conditions are specified then the situation is similar to what occurs at the two fixed lines on the boundary of $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ to define two BCFT2s: timelike geodesics that would normally cross this horizon in finite proper time cannot do so now due to the boundary conditions.

Since $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ and $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ are derived by foliating the same $\mathbb{R}^{2,5}$ lightcone, they contain conformally flat patches that are also conformal to each other [40]. Specifically, thiese conformally flat patches correspond to the Rindler wedge of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ and the static patch of ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ [39].

The Rindler wedge of orientable or non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ has metric,

$$ ds^{2}=-\left(\frac{r^{2}}{l^{2}}-1\right){\text{d}}t^{2}+\left(\frac{r^{2}}{l^{2}}\right)^{-1}{\text{d}}r^{2}+r^{2}{\text{d}}\phi^{2}+l^{2}{\text{d}}\Omega_{2}^{2}, $$

where $r\in(0,\ell)$ , $t\in\mathbb{R}$ , $\phi\in[0,2\pi)$ , and ${\text{d}}\Omega_{2}^{2}$ is the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ metric. The static patch metric of orientable ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ or $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ is

$$ ds^{2}=-\left(1-\frac{R^{2}}{L^{2}}\right){\text{d}}t^{2}+\left(1-\frac{R^{2}}{L^{2}}\right)^{-1}{\text{d}}R^{2}+R^{2}{\text{d}}\Omega_{2}^{2}+L^{2}{\text{d}}\phi^{2}. $$

where $R\in(0,L)$ , $t\in\mathbb{R}$ , $\phi\in[0,2\pi)$ , and ${\text{d}}\Omega_{2}^{2}$ is the ${\text{S}^{2}}$ metric. Multiplying Eq. 44 with $\ell/r=R/L$ conformally maps it to Eq. 43 (see Appendix E for more details). These patches can be fully contained in the Poincaré patches of either the orientable and non-orientable ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ , or ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ and $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ . (In the $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ case, we coordinatize the antipodal static patch with domain $-L\geq R\geq 0$ instead of $0\leq R\leq L$ .)

Note that the conformal map is strictly between a Rindler patch of the universal cover of the ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ spacetime and a static patch of the ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ spacetime, or in the non-orientable case, between a Rindler patch of the orientable infinite cover of $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ obtained by unwrapping $t$ and a static patch of $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ . This is because in ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ spacetime the future and past static patch horizons are independent and timelike separated. If the single cover of ${\text{AdS}_{3}}\times{\text{S}^{2}}$ or $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ were considered, this property would be violated under the conformal map by their closed timelike curves.

Since the conformal map is between a single Rindler wedge and static patch, in general it is only useful for conformally defining a static patch vacuum. Extending the static patch vacuum to a global vacuum is not possible with two separate conformal maps if the former involves entanglement between states defined on antipodal static patches. However, for $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ and $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ , this is not the case. Specifically, $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ actually consists of two distinct spacetimes separated by a lightlike singularity, which are not entangled with each other (i.e. any shared boundary conditions on the singularity must be Dirichlet boundary conditions). As a result, two separate conformal maps can map the separable conformal vacuum state of $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ piecewise from each Rindler wedge to each antipodal static patch in $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ .

This means that $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ supports the same conformal vacuum as the orientable infinite cover of $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ . Namely, $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ ’s conformal vacuum bulk state is $\left|\omega\right\rangle\left|\bar{\omega}\right\rangle$ , where $\left|\omega\right\rangle$ and $\left|\bar{\omega}\right\rangle$ are defined on antipodal static patches.

## IV Discussion

We found that the Rindler boundary state of ${\text{NO-AdS}_{3}}$ with unwrapped $t$ dimension has vanishing Hagedorn temperature due to supporting an infinitely long string. This must also be true for $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ . Since the conformal map preserves this property, this means that the $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ conformal vacuum state is unstable to excitation. It is expected that this false vacuum state decays to a true vacuum that should have a bulk geometry with the same asymptotic boundaries.

${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ has the same boundaries as $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ , except that its past and future boundary are similarly oriented. As a result, it is a prospective true vacuum bulk geometry. If it is the correct state, then this suggests that under perturbation $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ ’s vanishing Hagedorn temperature is surpassed and the state undergoes decay through a phase transition to ${\text{dS}_{4}}\times{\mathbb{R}}$ , corresponding to “untwisting” its oppositely oriented boundaries. We leave determining the validity of such a decay pathway, and its mechanism, for future work.

It is important to note that the added $\mathbb{R}$ dimension in $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ is crucial for connecting its vacuum with holography. While one could, in principle, construct a factorized vacuum on the space ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ with oppositely oriented boundaries it would be unclear how to infer anything about its holography. Furthermore, since $\text{NO-(AdS}_{3}\times{\text{S}^{2}}\text{)}$ has a well-understood spectrum, the additional ${\mathbb{R}}$ product space may allow for this conformal relationship to be used to determine the (excited-state) spectrum of $\text{OB-dS}_{4}\times\mathbb{R}$ as well.

Finally, there is an interesting observation about the uniqueness of this ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ vacuum’s construction from three dimensional ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ . It is well known that ${\text{AdS}_{3}}$ is uniquely able to be described as a purely topological gauge theory [53, 54]. It is also only in three dimensions that the black hole of negatively curved spacetime, the BTZ spacetime, can be defined. Similarly, as we have pointed out throughout its derivation, it is only in three dimensions that a non-orientable AdS can be defined that is geometrically indistinguishable from regular AdS, i.e. an orientifold of a double cover of AdS. In summary, it is these three spacetimes which are uniquely possible to define only in three dimensions that form the backbone of the conformal spectrum of the ${\text{dS}_{4}}$ vacuum.
